series.name: Ontological Characteristics
series.description: Discovers, classifies, refines, and validates the entities, categories, attributes, and boundaries of the domain.

open_ended.text: What are the primary entities, objects, concepts, or actors that exist in this domain? List them with brief descriptions.

follow_up_choices.text: Fewer than 5 core entities — the domain is compact and well-bounded
5–10 entities — moderate complexity with clear boundaries
10–20 entities — rich domain with distinct sub-areas
20+ entities — large domain requiring hierarchical organization
Uncertain — exploration may reveal entities not yet known

open_ended.text: What attributes, properties, or state define each entity? How do entities differ from one another?

follow_up_choices.text: 1–2 key attributes per entity — simple identifiers suffice
3–5 attributes per entity — moderate descriptive richness
6–10 attributes per entity — detailed characterization
10+ attributes per entity — comprehensive with optional fields
Highly variable — attributes differ significantly across entities

open_ended.text: What natural categories, types, or groupings organize these entities? Are there clear taxonomies or classification schemes?

follow_up_choices.text: A single flat list — no meaningful sub-groupings
2–3 broad categories partitioning the entities
A shallow hierarchy (2 levels deep) of types and subtypes
A deep hierarchy (3+ levels) with inheritance
Multiple overlapping classification axes (e.g., by function and by scale)

open_ended.text: Of the entities listed, which are absolutely essential (core) and which are optional, derivative, or contextual (peripheral)?

follow_up_choices.text: Most entities are core — the domain has little extraneous surface area
Roughly equal split between core and peripheral entities
A small core (~20%) with a large periphery of optional or derived entities
Core/peripheral depends on use case — context-dependent classification
Entities exist on a spectrum of centrality — no sharp core/peripheral boundary

open_ended.text: At what level of granularity should entities be modeled? Should fine distinctions be separate entities or attributes of coarser ones?

follow_up_choices.text: Coarse-grained — entities are broad; most variation is captured via attributes
Moderate — key specializations become distinct entities
Fine-grained — every meaningful distinction yields a separate entity
Mixed — core domains are fine-grained; peripheral domains are coarse
Undecided — granularity should emerge from relationship analysis

open_ended.text: How do entities relate to each other in terms of sharing, inheriting, or differentiating attributes?

follow_up_choices.text: Mostly independent — entities share few attributes beyond common identifiers
Shared attributes grouped by category — entities in same category share a profile
Inheritance hierarchy — subtypes inherit and extend parent attributes
Mixin / trait composition — entities compose attribute sets from multiple sources
Dynamic — attribute sharing depends on entity state or context

open_ended.text: What are the systemic boundaries of this domain? What is explicitly in scope vs. out of scope?

follow_up_choices.text: Tightly bounded — scope is narrow and well-defined
Moderately bounded — clear core with some fuzzy edges
Loosely bounded — domain bleeds into adjacent areas
Bounded by role/perspective — different stakeholders draw different boundaries
Boundaries are discovered — scoping is itself a goal of the process

open_ended.text: What external entities, systems, or actors interact with this domain but are not part of it?

follow_up_choices.text: No external interactions — fully self-contained domain
1–3 external actors (users, upstream data sources, downstream consumers)
4–7 external actors with distinct interaction patterns
8+ external actors — the domain is a hub in a larger ecosystem
External actors are themselves complex systems requiring partial modeling

open_ended.text: What is the lifecycle of each entity? How are they created, modified, combined, retired?

follow_up_choices.text: Simple lifecycle — create, read, update, delete (CRUD)
Stateful lifecycle — entities pass through defined states with transition rules
Versioned lifecycle — entities have history, revisions, or snapshots
Composite lifecycle — entities are assembled/disassembled from sub-entities
Evolving lifecycle — entities change type or role over time

open_ended.text: Are there entities that are missing from the model so far? What gaps exist in the current entity list?

follow_up_choices.text: No gaps — the current entity list is comprehensive
Minor gaps — 1–2 entities that were initially overlooked
Moderate gaps — several entities uncovered during analysis
Uncertain — the entity list needs validation against real-world instances
Incremental — entities will be added as the domain is explored further

open_ended.text: Which entities should be merged, split, or reclassified? Are there boundary cases where entity distinctions break down?

follow_up_choices.text: No changes needed — current classification is sound
1–2 entities need merging or splitting
Several entities could be refined, but classification is directionally correct
Significant restructuring needed — initial classification was exploratory
Ongoing — classification will stabilize as boundary cases are examined

open_ended.text: What constraints, invariants, or business rules apply to entity instances? What must always be true?

follow_up_choices.text: Minimal constraints — entities have few invariants beyond uniqueness
Moderate constraints — several required fields and validity rules
Strict constraints — entities must satisfy complex invariants at all times
Context-dependent — constraints vary by entity state or relationship
Evolving — constraints will be discovered through usage patterns

open_ended.text: What edge cases, exceptions, or degenerate cases could break the entity model? How should they be handled?

follow_up_choices.text: Few edge cases — the model is robust to real-world variation
Known edge cases — they are well-understood and can be handled explicitly
Many edge cases — the model needs to be flexible to accommodate them
Edge cases are domain-specific — they vary by deployment or context
Edge cases will emerge — the model should accommodate undefined unknowns

open_ended.text: How do entities compose or aggregate into larger structures? Can entities contain or be composed of other entities?

follow_up_choices.text: Flat — entities do not compose; all entities are atomic
Containment — some entities serve as containers for others (1-level deep)
Nested composition — entities form trees or recursive structures
Cross-cutting aggregation — entities participate in multiple overlapping groups
Dynamic composition — composition structure depends on entity state or context

open_ended.text: What are the cardinality and multiplicity relationships between entity types? Can an entity have zero, one, or many of another?

follow_up_choices.text: Mostly one-to-one — entities pair uniquely
One-to-many — common pattern with one parent referencing multiple children
Many-to-many — entities have complex cross-referencing patterns
Mixed — cardinalities vary significantly across entity pairs
Conditional — cardinalities depend on entity state or relationship type
